title: How to Build a Two-Phase Retirement Plan (Pre-65 and Post-65)
description: Structuring your finances around the 'Medicare Bridge'.
content:
Retirement is not a single, static phase. It has two distinct financial chapters: 'Pre-65' and 'Post-65'. The dividing line is Medicare eligibility. Before 65, you must self-fund healthcare (often $15,000-$25,000/year) and bridge the gap to Social Security. After 65, your fixed costs drop significantly as Medicare kicks in and Social Security checks arrive. Failing to plan for the expensive 'Phase 1' is the primary reason early retirees run out of cash. This guide helps you structure a 'Bridge Fund' to survive the gap.

Key Takeaways

  • The Expense Cliff: Your spending will likely drop by 20-30% at age 65. You don't need a portfolio that supports peak spending forever; you just need enough cash to cover the expensive years (55-65).
  • The Bridge Fund: Create a specific bucket of liquid assets (Cash/Brokerage) dedicated solely to paying health insurance premiums until Medicare starts. Do not count this money toward your long-term withdrawal rate.
  • Roth Conversions in Phase 1: Phase 1 often comes with lower taxable income (no wages, no RMDs, no Social Security). Use this window to convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at a low tax rate.
  • Social Security Timing: Use your portfolio to fund Phase 1 so you can delay Social Security until Phase 2 (age 70). This buys you a higher guaranteed income floor for late life.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The Affordable Care Act (ACA) provides subsidies based on income. In Phase 1, managing your 'Modified Adjusted Gross Income' (MAGI) is critical. By living on cash or Roth withdrawals, you can keep MAGI low and get insurance for cheap, effectively lowering the cost of Phase 1.

The Tale of Two Budgets

Scenario: Couple retiring at 58.

Phase 1: The Bridge (Age 58-65)

  • Healthcare: $24,000/year (Private Insurance/ACA).
  • Travel/Fun: $20,000/year ('Go-Go' years).
  • Living: $40,000/year.
  • Total Burn: $84,000/year.
  • Income Sources: 100% Portfolio Withdrawals.

Phase 2: The Senior Years (Age 65+)

  • Healthcare: $8,000/year (Medicare Premiums + Medigap). Cost drops $16k.
  • Travel: $10,000/year (Slowing down).
  • Living: $40,000/year.
  • Total Burn: $58,000/year.
  • Income Sources: Social Security ($35k) + Portfolio ($23k).

The Verdict: You need a portfolio that can support $84k for 7 years, but only $23k for the rest of your life. Don't panic if your withdrawal rate is high in Phase 1; it's temporary.

Asset Allocation by Phase

  1. Cash Heavy Early: Keep 3-5 years of expenses in Cash/Bonds for Phase 1. You cannot afford Sequence of Returns risk while your burn rate is high.
  2. Equity Heavy Late: Since Phase 2 has a guaranteed floor (Social Security), your remaining portfolio can be more aggressive (Stocks) to fight inflation and leave a legacy.
  3. HSA Utilization: Save your HSA for Phase 2 (Medicare premiums). Use cash for Phase 1 to keep taxable income low for subsidies.
  4. Debt Payoff: Try to enter Phase 2 mortgage-free. Eliminating the mortgage at 65 aligns perfectly with the drop in healthcare costs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I claim Social Security at 62 to help with Phase 1?

Mathematically, no. Spending down your assets to delay Social Security buys you a higher, safer income floor for Phase 2. It reduces longevity risk.

What if I get sick in Phase 1?

Max out your Out-of-Pocket limit. Ensure you have a 'Medical Emergency Fund' of ~$15,000 on top of your living expenses.

Can I work part-time in Phase 1?

Yes. Earning $20,000/year covers the healthcare cost, making Phase 1 much cheaper. This is 'Barista FIRE'.
